name: Say's Law
statement: Producing a good creates the income and means to buy other goods.
statementAccent: the income and means to buy
meaning: To buy, you must first produce something to sell, or earn income by producing. So the act of production generates the purchasing power that funds demand elsewhere — which is why the classical school held that an economy-wide glut, a general shortfall of demand for everything at once, could not persist.
mechanism: In a barter-like view, you produce in order to exchange, and money is only a temporary medium — 'the only way of getting rid of money is in the purchase of some product'. Every act of supply therefore constitutes demand for something else, so aggregate production and aggregate demand are linked at the source. On this reasoning a general glut is impossible; gluts can only be relative — too much of one thing relative to another — and are corrected by prices and reallocation.

examples.text: A baker who bakes a hundred loaves generates income — to workers, suppliers, and self — enough to buy those loaves and other goods too. On Say's reasoning a simultaneous oversupply of everything cannot last; only particular markets can be out of balance.

The 1930s became the great real-world argument: Keynesians read mass unemployment and unsold output as proof that aggregate demand can fall short for years, contradicting the law, while defenders held that markets self-correct in the long run.

If people save a large share of income and it is not re-spent or invested, demand can fall below what production created — unsold inventory, layoffs, recession — the shortfall Say's law rules out and Keynes insisted was real.

variants.name: The law of markets
variants.text: Say's own name for the doctrine — the loi des débouchés, or law of outlets — before it acquired its English slogan.

variants.name: 'Demand creates its own supply'
variants.text: The Keynesian inversion, sometimes called Keynes's law: in the short run, with idle capacity, output is driven by aggregate demand rather than the other way round.

whyItMatters: It sits at the fault line of macroeconomics. Whether production automatically generates enough demand to absorb it — or whether demand can chronically fall short — is the difference between the classical and Keynesian views of recessions, and it still shapes how economists argue about slumps and stimulus.

working.text: 'supply creates its own demand' is a later paraphrase, not Say's words; his actual claim was the milder one that production generates income to spend.
the law holds if income earned in production returns as spending; it fails to the extent that money is hoarded rather than spent or invested.
Say allowed that particular markets can overshoot; the contested claim is only that all markets cannot be glutted at once.

limits: It is a genuinely contested proposition, not a settled fact or theorem. Keynes's central attack in The General Theory (1936) was that demand can fall short of full-employment output because money can be hoarded rather than spent or invested, so general gluts and involuntary unemployment are possible and markets need not self-correct promptly. Its validity depends on contested assumptions about whether money is merely a medium of exchange and whether wages and prices adjust freely. Both the law and its Keynesian refutation remain live in macroeconomic debate.
misreadings: The famous 'supply creates its own demand' is a later paraphrase — popularised by Keynes, not written by Say — and it overstates a subtler claim: that producing generates the income to buy. Say himself acknowledged that particular markets can glut; the disputed part is only the impossibility of a general one.
origin: Formulated by the French classical economist Jean-Baptiste Say in his Treatise on Political Economy (1803) as the loi des débouchés, the law of markets, with related statements by James and John Stuart Mill. The pithy 'supply creates its own demand' does not appear in Say's own writing; it was popularised by John Maynard Keynes in 1936, though even Keynes seems to have been quoting an already-current phrase whose exact origin is unclear.

sources.text: Say, J.-B. (1803). A Treatise on Political Economy (Traité d'économie politique). — the law of markets.
